name: Crab Nebula
desc: The remains of the supernova seen from Earth in 1054, with a pulsar spinning 30 times a second at its heart. Small telescopes show a faint oval glow; larger ones under dark skies hint at its ragged, filamentary edges.

name: M 2
desc: A rich, compact globular cluster in Aquarius. Binoculars show a fuzzy star; an 8-inch telescope resolves its outer halo into a swarm of faint stars around a bright, dense core.

name: M 3
desc: One of the finest globular clusters, with about half a million stars and more known variable stars than any other. A 4-inch telescope starts to resolve its edges; larger ones show a sparkling ball with a bright core.

name: M 4
desc: One of the nearest globular clusters, about 7,200 light-years away, and among the easiest to resolve: small telescopes show individual stars and a bar of stars across its center. It lies just west of Antares.

name: M 5
desc: A large, bright globular cluster that rivals M13, easy in binoculars with the star 5 Serpentis just to its south-southeast. Medium apertures resolve a dense core surrounded by long arcs of stars.

name: Butterfly Cluster
desc: A bright open cluster whose stars outline a butterfly with open wings. Its brightest member, the orange giant BM Scorpii, stands out among the blue-white stars; best in binoculars or at low power.

name: Ptolemy's Cluster
desc: A large, brilliant open cluster near the Scorpion's tail, visible to the naked eye and recorded by Ptolemy around AD 130. It spans more than two full Moons, so binoculars or a wide-field eyepiece frame it best.

name: Lagoon Nebula
desc: A bright emission nebula visible to the naked eye from dark sites, crossed by a dark lane (the 'lagoon') with the young cluster NGC 6530 on its eastern side. A UHC filter brings out the gas and the bright Hourglass region near its western end.

name: M 9
desc: A small, fairly concentrated globular cluster near the center of the Milky Way, dimmed and reddened by dust. Medium apertures begin to resolve its outer stars.

name: M 10
desc: A bright globular cluster in Ophiuchus, about 14,000 light-years away. Binoculars show it in the same sweep as its near-twin M12, 3° away, and a 6-inch telescope resolves its outskirts.

name: Wild Duck Cluster
desc: One of the richest and most compact open clusters, with nearly 3,000 stars; the brightest form a V like a flight of ducks. A superb sight at medium power, set against the Scutum Star Cloud.

name: M 12
desc: A looser globular cluster than its neighbor M10, 3° away; its relatively sparse core makes it easy to resolve in medium apertures.

name: Hercules Globular Cluster
desc: The Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, the finest in the northern sky: binoculars show a bright fuzzy ball, and a 6-inch telescope resolves hundreds of stars. It lies on the western side of the Keystone asterism.

name: M 14
desc: A large but rather faint globular cluster in a sparse part of Ophiuchus. It looks evenly grainy; its stars are faint, so it needs about 8 inches of aperture to resolve.

name: M 15
desc: A bright, very dense globular cluster whose core has collapsed, giving it a tiny, intense center at any magnification. It also holds Pease 1, the first planetary nebula found inside a globular cluster.

name: Eagle Nebula
desc: A young star cluster inside the Eagle Nebula, home of the 'Pillars of Creation' photographed by Hubble. Small telescopes show the cluster easily; the nebula and its dark pillars need dark skies and a UHC or OIII filter.

name: Omega Nebula
desc: One of the brightest nebulae in the sky: a glowing bar with a hook at one end, which gives it the Swan, Omega and Checkmark names. Striking even in small telescopes, it responds superbly to a UHC or OIII filter.

name: M 18
desc: A small, sparse open cluster of a couple of dozen stars, lying between the Omega Nebula (M17) and the Small Sagittarius Star Cloud (M24).

name: M 19
desc: One of the most oblate globular clusters known, visibly oval in a telescope. It lies close to the center of the Milky Way, behind a veil of dust.

name: Trifid Nebula
desc: A young star-forming nebula split into three lobes by dark dust lanes, with a blue reflection nebula to its north. A UHC filter helps the red emission part but dims the blue reflection lobe, which is best seen unfiltered.

name: M 21
desc: A compact, young open cluster just northeast of the Trifid Nebula (M20); the two share a low-power field.

name: M 22
desc: One of the brightest globular clusters, visible to the naked eye from dark sites and among the nearest at about 10,000 light-years. Even small telescopes resolve its brightest stars; it sits low for northern observers but is well worth catching.

name: M 23
desc: A rich, scattered open cluster of about 150 stars in a busy Milky Way field, a fine sight in binoculars or at low power.

name: Small Sagittarius Star Cloud
desc: A bright patch of the Milky Way about 2° long, seen through a window in the dust onto stars thousands of light-years beyond. Sweep it with binoculars; it also contains the small cluster NGC 6603 and dark nebulae such as Barnard 92 and 93.

name: M 25
desc: A large, bright open cluster that is easy in binoculars. It contains the Cepheid variable U Sagittarii, which brightens and fades every 6.7 days.

name: M 26
desc: A small, modest open cluster near the Scutum Star Cloud, often overlooked in favor of its bright neighbor, the Wild Duck Cluster (M11).

name: Dumbbell Nebula
desc: One of the brightest planetary nebulae, easy in binoculars as a small glowing patch. Telescopes show its 'apple core' or hourglass shape, and an OIII filter reveals the fainter wings that round it into a football.

name: M 28
desc: A fairly compact globular cluster about 1° northwest of Lambda Sagittarii (Kaus Borealis), the star at the top of the Teapot's lid.

name: M 29
desc: A small open cluster in Cygnus whose brightest stars form a squat box, nicknamed the Cooling Tower; it lies less than 2° south of Gamma Cygni (Sadr) in a rich Milky Way field.

name: M 30
desc: A dense globular cluster in Capricornus whose core has collapsed; medium telescopes show a bright, compact center with chains of stars around it.

name: Andromeda Galaxy
desc: The nearest large spiral galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away and the most distant object easy to see with the naked eye. Binoculars show its long, bright core; telescopes add its companions M32 and M110 and, under dark skies, a dust lane.

name: M 32
desc: A small, bright elliptical satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy that looks like a fuzzy star just south of M31's core.

name: Triangulum Galaxy
desc: The third-largest galaxy of the Local Group, a face-on spiral about twice the width of the full Moon. Its light is spread thin, so it needs dark skies and low power; then its arms and the bright star-forming region NGC 604 appear.

name: M 34
desc: A bright, scattered open cluster in Perseus, easy in binoculars and lovely at low power.

name: M 35
desc: A large, rich open cluster at the feet of Gemini, visible to the naked eye from dark sites. The small, much more distant cluster NGC 2158 shares the low-power field.

name: M 36
desc: The most compact of the three bright open clusters in Auriga (M36, M37 and M38): a tight group of about 60 young stars.

name: M 37
desc: The richest of the Auriga clusters: a dense swarm of hundreds of faint stars with an orange star near its center, beautiful in any telescope.

name: M 38
desc: A large open cluster in Auriga whose stars form a cross or starfish pattern; the small cluster NGC 1907 lies just to its south.

name: M 39
desc: A large, loose open cluster in Cygnus, best in binoculars or at very low power, where its bright stars form a triangle.

name: M 40
desc: Not a nebula or cluster but a pair of unrelated stars, Winnecke 4, which Messier logged while looking for a nebula reported in this area; it stays in the catalogue by tradition. Its components (magnitudes 9.7 and 10.2; spectral types G0 (yellow) and F8 (yellow-white)) lie 53.2″ apart at PA 76° (measured 2017).

name: M 41
desc: A bright open cluster 4° south of Sirius, visible to the naked eye from dark sites, with a reddish giant star near its center.

name: Orion Nebula
desc: One of the brightest nebulae in the sky, visible to the naked eye as the middle 'star' of Orion's sword and about 1,300 light-years away. Even small telescopes show glowing wings of gas around the Trapezium, the young stars that make it shine.

name: De Mairan's Nebula
desc: A comma-shaped part of the Orion Nebula complex, separated from M42 by a dark lane and lit by the young star NU Orionis at its center.

name: Beehive Cluster
desc: Praesepe, the Beehive: a large open cluster visible to the naked eye as a misty patch in Cancer, about 600 light-years away. Binoculars resolve dozens of stars and frame it best.

name: Pleiades
desc: The Seven Sisters, the brightest and most famous star cluster, about 440 light-years away. Binoculars show dozens of blue-white stars; the nebulosity around them, a dust cloud the cluster is passing through, is faint to the eye but shines in photographs.

name: M 46
desc: A rich, even cluster of hundreds of faint stars. The planetary nebula NGC 2438 appears on its northern side, though it is probably unrelated to the cluster.

name: M 47
desc: A bright, coarse open cluster near M46, visible to the naked eye under dark skies; its few dozen bright stars contrast with M46's rich, faint swarm in the same binocular field.

name: M 48
desc: A large open cluster in Hydra, faintly visible to the naked eye from dark sites and well framed by binoculars.

name: M 49
desc: The brightest galaxy of the Virgo Cluster, a giant elliptical that shows as a bright oval glow with a star-like core.

name: M 50
desc: A bright open cluster in Monoceros, often described as heart-shaped, about a third of the way from Sirius to Procyon.

name: Whirlpool Galaxy
desc: The classic face-on spiral, interacting with its smaller companion NGC 5195. It was the first galaxy whose spiral structure was recognized (Lord Rosse, 1845), and its arms can be glimpsed in an 8-inch telescope under dark skies.

name: M 52
desc: A rich, compact open cluster in Cassiopeia; the faint Bubble Nebula (NGC 7635) lies about 35′ to its southwest.

name: M 53
desc: A compact globular cluster in Coma Berenices, one of the more remote in the Messier list at about 60,000 light-years. The faint, loose globular NGC 5053 lies 1° to its southeast.

name: M 54
desc: A small, bright globular cluster about 87,000 light-years away that belongs to the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy, not to the Milky Way — so Messier's 1778 discovery was, unknowingly, the first globular cluster found in another galaxy.

name: M 55
desc: A large, loose globular cluster low in Sagittarius; its sparse core makes it easy to resolve in small telescopes.

name: M 56
desc: A small globular cluster set in a rich Milky Way star field midway between Albireo and Gamma Lyrae (Sulafat).

name: Ring Nebula
desc: The classic smoke-ring planetary nebula, a shell of gas cast off by a dying star. Even a small telescope shows the oval ring between Beta and Gamma Lyrae; its faint central white dwarf is a test for large apertures.

name: M 58
desc: One of the brightest barred spirals of the Virgo Cluster, showing an oval glow with a brighter center.

name: M 59
desc: An elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, sharing a medium-power field with M60.

name: M 60
desc: A giant elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster; the small spiral NGC 4647 appears to touch its edge.

name: M 61
desc: One of the largest spirals in the Virgo Cluster, seen face-on; large telescopes show hints of arms around its bright core. Several supernovae have been seen in it.

name: M 62
desc: A bright, dense globular cluster near the center of the Milky Way, visibly lopsided because of the galaxy's tidal pull.

name: Sunflower Galaxy
desc: A bright spiral whose short, patchy arms give it the look of a sunflower in photographs; telescopes show an oval glow with a bright, star-like nucleus.

name: Black Eye Galaxy
desc: A bright spiral with a dark band of dust across one side of its nucleus — the 'black eye' — which medium telescopes can show.

name: M 65
desc: A bright, tilted spiral in the Leo Triplet, sharing a low-power field with M66 and NGC 3628.

name: M 66
desc: The brightest member of the Leo Triplet, a spiral distorted by its neighbors; it looks broader and more mottled than M65 beside it.

name: M 67
desc: One of the oldest known open clusters, about 4 billion years old: a rich field of faint stars, easy in binoculars near Acubens (Alpha Cancri).

name: M 68
desc: A globular cluster in Hydra, low for northern observers; medium telescopes resolve its outer stars around a moderately concentrated core.

name: M 69
desc: A small, bright globular cluster near the Teapot's base in Sagittarius, 2.5° west of its near-twin M70.

name: M 70
desc: A small, dense globular cluster near the Teapot's base whose core has collapsed, 2.5° east of M69. Comet Hale–Bopp was discovered next to it in 1995.

name: M 71
desc: A loose, faint globular cluster in Sagitta that was long classed as an open cluster; small telescopes resolve it easily.

name: M 72
desc: A faint, remote globular cluster in Aquarius, about 55,000 light-years away, appearing as a small, round fuzzy patch.

name: M 73
desc: Four stars in Aquarius forming a small Y. Messier logged it as a cluster with nebulosity, but the stars are unrelated and lie at different distances.

name: Phantom Galaxy
desc: A grand-design spiral seen face-on, beautiful in photographs but one of the hardest Messier objects to see: its light is spread thin, so it needs dark skies and low power.

name: M 75
desc: A small, very concentrated globular cluster about 68,000 light-years away, one of the more remote Messier globulars.

name: Little Dumbbell Nebula
desc: A planetary nebula in Perseus that looks like a tiny version of M27, with two lobes; it is one of the fainter Messier objects, and an OIII filter helps.

name: M 77
desc: The brightest Seyfert galaxy, with an intensely bright active nucleus; telescopes show a compact oval glow around a star-like core.

name: M 78
desc: One of the brightest reflection nebulae in the sky: a fan of light in Orion, dust reflecting the light of two 10th-magnitude stars. It shines by reflected starlight, so nebula filters do not help.

name: M 79
desc: A compact globular cluster in Lepus, on the opposite side of the sky from the galactic center; it may have come from a dwarf galaxy absorbed by the Milky Way.

name: M 80
desc: One of the densest globular clusters, a bright, compressed ball midway between Antares and Acrab (Beta Scorpii); a nova flared in it in 1860.

name: Bode's Galaxy
desc: A bright grand-design spiral in Ursa Major, visible in binoculars as an oval glow with M82 just over half a degree away — together one of the best galaxy pairs in the sky.

name: Cigar Galaxy
desc: A starburst galaxy seen edge-on, slender and mottled by dust lanes; its burst of star formation was triggered by a close encounter with M81.

name: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
desc: A bright, face-on barred spiral in Hydra; large telescopes show its bar and arms. Six supernovae have been seen in it.

name: M 84
desc: A lenticular galaxy at the heart of the Virgo Cluster, at the western end of Markarian's Chain next to M86.

name: M 85
desc: A bright lenticular galaxy in Coma Berenices, the northernmost member of the Virgo Cluster; the barred spiral NGC 4394 lies nearby.

name: M 86
desc: A large elliptical or lenticular galaxy in Markarian's Chain, close to M84; it is approaching us, one of the few galaxies with a blueshift.

name: Virgo A
desc: The giant elliptical at the center of the Virgo Cluster, surrounded by thousands of globular clusters; its central black hole was the first ever imaged (2019). Telescopes show a round glow with a bright core; its jet is a challenge for large apertures.

name: M 88
desc: A multi-arm spiral in the Virgo Cluster, tilted so that it shows an elongated oval with a bright core.

name: M 89
desc: An almost perfectly round elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, looking like a fuzzy star at low power.

name: M 90
desc: A large spiral in the Virgo Cluster that is approaching us; it appears as an elongated glow, and its gas-poor arms form few new stars.

name: M 91
desc: A barred spiral in Coma Berenices, the faintest of the Messier galaxies; its bar shows as an elongated core.

name: M 92
desc: A bright globular cluster in Hercules with a dense core, often overlooked in favor of M13 although it is nearly as impressive.

name: M 93
desc: A bright, compact open cluster in Puppis whose brightest stars form a wedge or arrowhead.

name: M 94
desc: A bright spiral with an intense inner ring of star formation; small telescopes show a bright oval core in a fainter halo.

name: M 95
desc: A barred spiral in Leo whose bar shows as an elongated core in medium telescopes; it shares a low-power field with M96.

name: M 96
desc: The brightest galaxy of the Leo I Group, a spiral with an oval glow and a bright core, near M95 and M105.

name: Owl Nebula
desc: A large, round planetary nebula in Ursa Major whose two dark patches look like an owl's eyes in larger telescopes; an OIII filter helps. The edge-on galaxy M108 lies 48′ away.

name: M 98
desc: A nearly edge-on spiral in Coma Berenices that appears as a long, faint streak; it is approaching us.

name: Coma Pinwheel
desc: A face-on spiral in the Virgo Cluster with one longer, distorted arm; medium telescopes show a round glow with a hint of spiral structure.

name: M 100
desc: A large, face-on grand-design spiral in the Virgo Cluster; telescopes show a round glow with a bright core, and large apertures its two main arms.

name: Pinwheel Galaxy
desc: A large face-on spiral with low surface brightness: from dark sites binoculars show a faint round glow, and telescopes reveal knotty arms dotted with bright star-forming regions.

name: M 102
desc: Most likely the lenticular galaxy NGC 5866 (the Spindle), seen nearly edge-on with a dark dust lane along its length. Its identity is disputed: Méchain later called it a duplicate observation of M101.

name: M 103
desc: A small, bright open cluster in Cassiopeia shaped like a fan or arrowhead, about 1° from Delta Cassiopeiae (Ruchbah).

name: Sombrero Galaxy
desc: A nearly edge-on spiral with a huge central bulge and a dark dust lane — visible in medium telescopes — that give it the look of a broad-brimmed hat.

name: M 105
desc: An elliptical galaxy in the Leo I Group, a round glow with a bright core near M95 and M96.

name: M 106
desc: A large, bright spiral in Canes Venatici with an active nucleus; telescopes show an elongated glow with a bright core, and photographs reveal extra 'anomalous' arms.

name: M 107
desc: A loose globular cluster in Ophiuchus, easy to resolve in medium apertures; Helen Sawyer Hogg added it to the Messier list in 1947.

name: M 108
desc: An edge-on barred spiral in Ursa Major, a mottled sliver of light 48′ from the Owl Nebula (M97); the two make a fine pair.

name: M 109
desc: A barred spiral in Ursa Major just southeast of Phecda (Gamma Ursae Majoris); its bar shows as an elongated core in medium telescopes.

name: M 110
desc: A large elliptical satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, fainter and more diffuse than M32, northwest of M31's core; it was the last object added to the Messier list, in 1966.

name: Cave Nebula
desc: A faint emission nebula in Cepheus with a dark 'cave mouth' along one side; it needs dark skies and a UHC filter.

name: Double Cluster
desc: Two bright open clusters, NGC 869 and NGC 884, side by side in the same low-power field. Visible to the naked eye as a hazy patch between Perseus and Cassiopeia, they are among the finest sights for binoculars.

name: Hyades
desc: The nearest open cluster to the Sun, about 150 light-years away, forming the V-shaped face of Taurus. Orange Aldebaran lies in front of it but is not a member.

name: Coalsack Nebula
desc: The most prominent dark nebula in the sky, a dust cloud about 600 light-years away that blots out the Milky Way beside the Southern Cross; best seen with the naked eye.

name: Bow-Tie Nebula
desc: A planetary nebula in Cepheus around an 11th-magnitude Wolf–Rayet central star, appearing as a small oval glow with brighter edges.

name: NGC 45
desc: A 10.4-magnitude weakly barred spiral galaxy (SABd) in Cetus, about 6.2′ × 4.4′.

name: String of Pearls Galaxy
desc: A large, bright edge-on galaxy in Sculptor, irregular and mottled; one of the nearest galaxies beyond the Local Group.

name: NGC 103
desc: A 9.8-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 2.7′ across.

name: 47 Tucanae
desc: The second-brightest globular cluster after Omega Centauri, visible to the naked eye beside the Small Magellanic Cloud; a superb sight with a dense, bright core.

name: NGC 129
desc: A 6.5-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 5.4′ across.

name: NGC 133
desc: A 9.4-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 2.1′ across.

name: NGC 134
desc: A 10.3-magnitude weakly barred spiral galaxy (SABb) in Sculptor, about 8.4′ × 1.8′.

name: NGC 146
desc: A 9.1-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 3.6′ across.

name: NGC 147
desc: A dwarf spheroidal satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy; faint and diffuse, it needs dark skies and lies about 1° from its brighter sibling NGC 185.

name: NGC 185
desc: A dwarf elliptical satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, brighter and more compact than nearby NGC 147.

name: Polarissima Cluster
desc: One of the oldest open clusters known, about 7 billion years old, less than 5° from the north celestial pole; small telescopes show a faint, rich haze of stars.

name: NGC 189
desc: An 8.8-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 2.7′ across.

name: NGC 225
desc: A 7.0-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 4.2′ across.

name: Skull Nebula
desc: A large planetary nebula in Cetus, a faint ring with several stars inside it; an OIII filter helps.

name: NGC 247
desc: A large, nearly edge-on spiral in Cetus with low surface brightness, about 4° from the Sculptor Galaxy (NGC 253).

name: Sculptor Galaxy
desc: One of the brightest galaxies in the sky, a large, dusty starburst spiral seen nearly edge-on; binoculars show a long glow, and telescopes a mottled disc.

name: Pacman Nebula
desc: An emission nebula in Cassiopeia, about 35′ × 30′.

name: NGC 288
desc: An 8.1-magnitude globular cluster in Sculptor, about 9.6′ across. It lies about 29,000 light-years away.

name: Small Magellanic Cloud
desc: A 2.3-magnitude barred Magellanic spiral galaxy (SBm) in Tucana, about 5.0° × 3.0°.

name: Sculptor Pinwheel Galaxy
desc: A large, face-on spiral in Sculptor, faint and diffuse; it needs dark skies and low power.

name: NGC 330
desc: A 9.6-magnitude open cluster in Tucana, about 2.8′ × 2.5′.

name: NGC 362
desc: A bright globular cluster beside the Small Magellanic Cloud, though it lies far in the foreground, in our own galaxy, about 28,000 light-years away.

name: NGC 381
desc: A 9.3-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 6′ across.

name: NGC 419
desc: A 10.5-magnitude globular cluster in Tucana, about 2.8′ across.

name: NGC 436
desc: An 8.8-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 5.7′ across.

name: Owl Cluster
desc: A bright open cluster nicknamed the Owl or E.T. Cluster: two bright stars, including Phi Cassiopeiae, make the eyes, and rows of fainter stars the outstretched arms.

name: NGC 488
desc: A 10.3-magnitude spiral galaxy (Sb) in Pisces, about 5.1′ × 3.7′.

name: NGC 524
desc: A 10.3-magnitude lenticular galaxy (S0-a) in Pisces, about 3.4′ across.

name: NGC 559
desc: A compact open cluster in Cassiopeia, a rich patch of faint stars in small telescopes.

name: NGC 584
desc: A 10.3-magnitude elliptical galaxy (E) in Cetus, about 3.8′ × 2.5′.

name: NGC 613
desc: A 10.3-magnitude spiral galaxy (Sbc) in Sculptor, about 5.5′ × 4.5′.

name: NGC 637
desc: An 8.2-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 4.5′ across.

name: NGC 654
desc: A 6.5-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 6.3′ across.

name: NGC 659
desc: A 7.9-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 4.2′ across.

name: NGC 663
desc: A bright, rich open cluster in Cassiopeia, one of the best in a constellation full of them, less than 2° east of M103.

name: NGC 676
desc: A 10.2-magnitude (B-band) lenticular galaxy (S0-a) in Pisces, about 2.8′ × 0.7′.

name: NGC 720
desc: A 10.1-magnitude elliptical galaxy (E) in Cetus, about 4.5′ × 2.4′.

name: NGC 744
desc: A 7.9-magnitude open cluster in Perseus, about 12′ across.

name: NGC 752
desc: A large, scattered open cluster in Andromeda, older than most at over a billion years; best in binoculars.

name: NGC 772
desc: A 10.3-magnitude spiral galaxy (Sb) in Aries, about 4.6′ × 2.5′.

name: h Persei Cluster
desc: h Persei, the western half of the Double Cluster (C14): a rich, bright open cluster that shares a low-power field with NGC 884.

name: Chi Persei Cluster
desc: Chi Persei, the eastern half of the Double Cluster (C14), with several red supergiants among its blue-white stars; it shares a low-power field with NGC 869.

name: Silver Sliver Galaxy
desc: A classic edge-on spiral in Andromeda: a thin silver sliver, split by a dark dust lane in larger telescopes under dark skies.

name: NGC 908
desc: A 10.3-magnitude weakly barred spiral galaxy (SABc) in Cetus, about 6.1′ × 2.8′.

name: NGC 925
desc: A 10.1-magnitude spiral galaxy (Scd) in Triangulum, about 11′ × 5.8′.

name: NGC 936
desc: A 10.2-magnitude lenticular galaxy (S0-a) in Cetus, about 4.4′ × 3.2′.

name: NGC 956
desc: An 8.9-magnitude open cluster in Andromeda, about 4.5′ across.

name: NGC 957
desc: A 7.6-magnitude open cluster in Perseus, about 10′ across.

name: NGC 1023
desc: A 9.5-magnitude elliptical/lenticular galaxy (E-S0) in Perseus, about 7.4′ × 3.1′.

name: NGC 1027
desc: A 6.7-magnitude open cluster in Cassiopeia, about 7.8′ across.

name: Fornax Dwarf Cluster 3
desc: A 13.6-magnitude (B-band) globular cluster in Fornax, about 1.2′ across.

name: NGC 1097
desc: A barred spiral in Fornax with a bright nucleus and a long bar; it has a small elliptical companion.

name: NGC 1232
desc: A 10.1-magnitude weakly barred spiral galaxy (SABc) in Eridanus, about 6.8′ × 5.8′.

name: NGC 1245
desc: An 8.4-magnitude open cluster in Perseus, about 11′ across.

name: NGC 1261
desc: A small, compact globular cluster in Horologium, about 53,000 light-years away, appearing as a round, softly glowing ball.

name: NGC 1269
desc: An 8.7-magnitude lenticular galaxy (S0-a) in Eridanus, about 11′ × 9.9′.

name: Perseus A
desc: The giant central galaxy of the Perseus Cluster and a powerful radio source (Perseus A); small telescopes show a faint smudge among other cluster galaxies.

name: NGC 1313
desc: A 9.5-magnitude barred spiral galaxy (SBcd) in Reticulum, about 11′ × 9.1′.

name: Fornax A
desc: An 8.5-magnitude lenticular galaxy (S0) in Fornax, about 13′ × 7.7′.

name: Fornax B
desc: A 10.9-magnitude weakly barred spiral galaxy (SABa) in Fornax, about 3.1′ × 2.6′.

name: NGC 1326
desc: A 10.4-magnitude lenticular galaxy (S0-a) in Fornax, about 4.3′ × 2.9′.

name: NGC 1332
desc: A 10.4-magnitude elliptical/lenticular galaxy (E-S0) in Eridanus, about 5.3′ × 3.8′.

name: NGC 1333
desc: A star cluster with nebulosity in Perseus, about 20′ across. Its catalogued magnitude, 10.9 (B-band), is that of the star cluster; the nebulosity is much fainter.

name: NGC 1340
desc: A 10.4-magnitude elliptical galaxy (E) in Fornax, about 5.1′ × 3.1′.

name: NGC 1342
desc: A 6.7-magnitude open cluster in Perseus, about 6.3′ across.

name: NGC 1350
desc: A 10.3-magnitude spiral galaxy (Sab) in Fornax, about 5.2′ × 2.6′.

name: NGC 1360
desc: A 9.4-magnitude planetary nebula in Fornax, about 6.4′ across. Its central star is magnitude 11.4.

name: NGC 1365
desc: A 10.1-magnitude spiral galaxy (Sb) in Fornax, about 12′ × 6.1′.

name: NGC 1380

Castor C (magnitude 9.8) lies 69.6″ away.

name: Cor Caroli
desc: An easy, attractive pair in Canes Venatici for any small telescope. Its components (magnitudes 2.9 and 5.5) lie 19.2″ apart at PA 229° (measured 2023).

name: Delta Cephei
desc: The prototype Cepheid variable (magnitude 3.5–4.4 every 5.4 days), with a wide bluish companion. Its components (magnitudes 4.2 and 6.1; spectral types F5 Iab (yellow-white) and B7 (blue-white)) lie 41″ apart at PA 192° (measured 2025).

name: Epsilon Lyrae (Double Double)
desc: The famous "Double Double" near Vega. ε¹'s components (magnitudes 5.2 and 6.1; spectral types A4 V (white) and F1 V (yellow-white)) lie 2.1″ apart at PA 342° (measured 2025). ε¹ and ε² are 209.4″ apart (easy in binoculars), and ε² splits into stars of magnitude 5.3 and 5.4, 2.4″ apart.

name: Eta Cassiopeiae
desc: A Sun-like star with a fainter, reddish companion. Its components (magnitudes 3.5 and 7.4; spectral types G1 V (yellow) and M (orange-red)) lie 13.6″ apart at PA 329° (predicted for 2027.0 from its 479-year orbit).

name: Eta Persei
desc: A cool supergiant with a faint bluish companion. Its components (magnitudes 3.8 and 8.5; spectral types M3 I (orange-red) and B9 V (blue-white)) lie 27.1″ apart at PA 301° (measured 2024).

name: Gamma Ceti
desc: A close, unequal pair — a good test for small telescopes. Its components (magnitudes 3.5 and 6.2; spectral types A2 V (white) and F4 V (yellow-white)) lie 1.9″ apart at PA 299° (measured 2024).

name: Gamma Delphini
desc: A lovely pair in Job's Coffin, the diamond of Delphinus. Its components (magnitudes 4.4 and 5.0; spectral types K1 IV (orange) and F7 V (yellow-white)) lie 8.8″ apart at PA 266° (measured 2025).

name: Iota Cancri
desc: A wide, easy color-contrast pair in Cancer, often compared to Albireo. Its components (magnitudes 4.1 and 6.6; spectral types G8 III (yellow) and A2 V (white)) lie 30.5″ apart at PA 308° (measured 2022).

name: Iota Orionis
desc: The brightest star of Orion’s sword, at its southern tip below the Orion Nebula: a brilliant primary with a much fainter companion. Its components (magnitudes 2.8 and 7.7) lie 11.2″ apart at PA 141° (measured 2023). A third star, C (magnitude 9.8), lies 49.3″ away.

name: Izar
desc: A beautiful but tight orange-and-blue pair that Struve called Pulcherrima, "the most beautiful"; it needs steady seeing. Its components (magnitudes 2.6 and 4.8) lie 2.9″ apart at PA 347° (measured 2024).

name: Mesarthim
desc: An easy pair of near-twin white stars, one of the first doubles discovered with a telescope (Robert Hooke, 1664). Its components (magnitudes 4.5 and 4.6; spectral types A2 IV (white) and B9 V (blue-white)) lie 7.3″ apart at PA 1° (measured 2024).

name: Mizar and Alcor
desc: The famous double in the handle of the Big Dipper; together with Alcor it forms a sextuple star system. Mizar A and B (magnitudes 2.2 and 3.9) lie 14.4″ apart at PA 153° (measured 2022). Alcor (magnitude 4.0) lies 715.5″ (11.9′) from Mizar, an easy naked-eye pair.

name: Nu Draconis
desc: A matched pair of white stars, easily split in binoculars. Its components (magnitudes 4.9 and 4.9; spectral types A4 (white) and A6 V (white)) lie 62.2″ apart at PA 308° (measured 2023).

name: Omicron¹ Cygni
desc: An orange giant with a bluish companion. Its components (magnitudes 3.9 and 7.0) lie 106.7″ apart at PA 173° (measured 2023). 30 Cygni (magnitude 4.8) lies 336.7″ away, completing a fine wide triple.

name: Polaris
desc: The North Star has a faint companion visible in small telescopes. Its components (magnitudes 2.0 and 9.1; spectral types F7 Ib (yellow-white) and F3 V (yellow-white)) lie 18.4″ apart at PA 236° (measured 2016).

name: Porrima
desc: A pair of near-identical white stars whose separation changes quickly: it was unsplittable around its 2005 periastron and is now widening. Its components (magnitudes 3.5 and 3.5; spectral types F0 V (yellow-white) and F0 V (yellow-white)) lie 3.66″ apart at PA 350° (predicted for 2027.0 from its 169-year orbit).

name: Psi¹ Piscium
desc: A wide, near-equal pair of white stars. Its components (magnitudes 5.3 and 5.5; spectral types B9.5 V (blue-white) and A0 V (white)) lie 30″ apart at PA 159° (measured 2025).

name: Rasalgethi
desc: A variable red supergiant whose companion looks greenish by contrast. Its components (magnitudes 3.5 and 5.4) lie 4.9″ apart at PA 101° (measured 2025).

name: Rigel
desc: The brilliant blue-white supergiant of Orion; its faint companion is a classic test of optics in the glare. Its components (magnitudes 0.3 and 6.8) lie 9.4″ apart at PA 204° (measured 2023).

name: Sigma Orionis
desc: A multiple star just southwest of Alnitak whose brightest member lights up IC 434, the glow behind the Horsehead. The bright pair σ Ori AB and companion D (magnitudes 3.8 and 6.6) lie 13.5″ apart at PA 84° (measured 2021). E (magnitude 6.3) lies 42″ away and C (magnitude 8.8) 11.4″ away.

name: Struve 747
desc: A wide, easy pair of blue-white stars in Orion’s sword, about half a degree south of the Orion Nebula and 8′ southwest of Iota Orionis. Its components (magnitudes 4.7 and 5.5; spectral types B0.5 V (blue-white) and B1 V (blue-white)) lie 35.3″ apart at PA 224° (measured 2021).

name: Trapezium
desc: The four bright young stars at the heart of the Orion Nebula (M42); the brightest, θ¹ Ori C, provides most of the ultraviolet light that makes the nebula glow. θ¹ Ori C and D (magnitudes 5.1 and 6.7; spectral types O7 V (blue) and B1.5 V (blue-white)) lie 13.8″ apart at PA 60° (measured 2021). A (magnitude 6.7) and B (8.0), both eclipsing binaries, complete the trapezoid, whose widest pair (A–D) spans 21.4″; the fainter E and F, near magnitude 11, need more aperture and steady air.

name: Xi Boötis
desc: A nearby binary of a yellow and an orange dwarf star. Its components (magnitudes 4.8 and 7.0; spectral types G8 V (yellow) and K5 V (orange)) lie 4.62″ apart at PA 286° (predicted for 2027.0 from its 152-year orbit).

name: Xi Ursae Majoris
desc: The first binary star to have its orbit calculated (Félix Savary, 1827). Its components (magnitudes 4.3 and 4.8; spectral types F9 V (yellow-white) and G9 V (yellow)) lie 2.74″ apart at PA 131° (predicted for 2027.0 from its 59.9-year orbit).

name: Zeta Aquarii
desc: A close, near-equal pair at the center of the Water Jar asterism. Its components (magnitudes 4.3 and 4.5) lie 2.48″ apart at PA 150° (predicted for 2027.0 from its 427-year orbit).

name: Zeta Lyrae
desc: A wide, easy pair at the corner of Lyra’s parallelogram, a fine stop on the way from Vega to the Double Double (ε Lyr). Its components (magnitudes 4.3 and 5.6) lie 43.7″ apart at PA 150° (measured 2025).
